Question ID: GEO_U04_L05_GP_Q01

MLA Standard: Readiness Support Only

A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. What is the hypotenuse?

feedback.text: Adding the legs gives 14, but the Pythagorean Theorem uses squares of side lengths.
The values must be squared before adding, so sqrt(14) does not match the theorem.
Multiplying the legs does not find the hypotenuse.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: GEO_U04_L05_GP_Q02

MLA Standard: Readiness Support Only

Which equation fits a right triangle with legs 5 and 12 and hypotenuse c?

feedback.text: The Pythagorean Theorem requires squaring both legs, not adding them directly.
The legs are squared and added to equal the hypotenuse squared.
This treats 12 as the hypotenuse, but c is identified as the hypotenuse.
The theorem uses a sum of squares, not a product of legs.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: GEO_U04_L05_GP_Q03

MLA Standard: Readiness Support Only

A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. What is the other leg?

feedback.text: Subtracting 5 from 13 ignores the squares in the Pythagorean Theorem.
Adding the squares would make a larger hypotenuse, but the hypotenuse is already 13.
Adding the known side lengths does not find a missing leg.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: GEO_U04_L05_GP_Q04

MLA Standard: Readiness Support Only

Which side is always opposite the right angle in a right triangle?

feedback.text: A leg forms the right angle; it is not opposite the right angle.
The shorter side may be a leg, but the side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse.
Adjacent depends on a chosen acute angle, not the right angle.
The hypotenuse is the longest side and is opposite the right angle.

Question ID: GEO_U04_L05_GP_Q05

MLA Standard: Readiness Support Only

Which set of side lengths can form a right triangle?

feedback.text: 9? + 12? = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15?, so the set forms a right triangle.
